VERDICT: ACCEPTI find no concrete counterexample to the theorem under the stated splice hypotheses and the previously established two-leg lemmas. The local receiver, charge-additivity, path/cycle, donor, quota, and zigzag arguments are mutually consistent.There are two dependencies that should be stated explicitly as inherited hypotheses of this extension:the earlier two-leg exclusion of the first three donor rules applies uniformly to every module and every allowed splice placement; and  the previously established degree-three matching criterion really excludes mixed promotion bundles, not only same-color bundles.With those dependencies, the extension is correct. The finite and Lean checks are unnecessary for the conclusions below.Receiver localityThe receiver-locality lemma is valid under the stated single-terminal feasibility condition.If a selected corner and an endpoint occupy opposite corners of a tile, the two intervening corners cannot be endpoints by the no-adjacency condition. They also cannot be selected, because each would then be adjacent to both the selected corner and the opposite endpoint. The endpoint consequently has two blank internal neighbors and at most two occupied exterior neighbors, so it cannot have the required occupied degree three.Therefore, whenever an endpoint-bearing tile contains a selected vertex, that selected vertex has an endpoint neighbor inside the same tile. Since selected vertices have a unique occupied endpoint neighbor, that endpoint is unique.The receiver-spill consequence also follows. If a retained support from module  $i$  lay in a tile belonging only to another module, its own unique endpoint neighbor would have to lie in the same tile by locality. That would make the tile belong to module  $i$  as well. Hence retained supports cannot silently enter another module’s receiver.Splice geometry and endpoint degreesThe splice assumptions are sufficient to preserve the endpoint geometry.A module has at most one port in any physical tile because its two ports are at Manhattan distance at least five. A port can have at most one foreign endpoint neighbor: one of its two original selected supports is consumed by the splice, while the hypothesis that no other original selected support becomes an endpoint rules out a second foreign endpoint at the other support position.Thus, if a tile contains endpoints from several modules, the module-incidence graph inside that tile has maximum degree one. Since the endpoint set in the tile is connected, the tile can represent only one intratile splice between two modules. Distinct intratile splices therefore occur in distinct tiles.The splice also preserves occupied endpoint degree three. A port loses one selected support and gains the other module’s endpoint at that site; the number of occupied neighbors remains three. The no-extra-endpoint-edge condition prevents unrelated modules from increasing that degree.Four alignment phasesThe charge arithmetic in the phase table is correct. With
$$h=\frac{a+b}{2},\qquad |M_i|=w+h-1,$$
the four rows give
$$\begin{aligned}
(h+4)+(w+h-1)-2\left(\frac w2+h+1\right)&=1,\\
h+(w+h-1)-2\left(\frac w2+h\right)&=-1,\\
(h+2)+(w+h-1)-2(w+h)&=1-w,\\
(h-2)+(w+h-1)-2(w+h-2)&=1-w.
\end{aligned}$$
Thus every isolated module has corrected charge  $+1$ ,  $-1$ , or  $1-w\le-5$ .The phase counts are also internally consistent with the two-leg geometry:row phase zero has a one-tile-row bar and contributes  $w/2+1$  or  $w/2$  bar tiles;row phase one has a two-tile-row bar and contributes  $w+2$  or  $w$ ;the remaining leg tiles contribute  $h$  or  $h-2$ ;the selected-support counts in the four rows give exactly the displayed charges.The assertion that the  $+1$  phase has both selected supports of each port inside the port tile is the key geometric fact used later for the positive-module exclusion and donor construction. It is consistent with the earlier two-leg pattern and is preserved by tile-preserving translations, rotations, and reflections.Charge additivity under splicingThe splice ledger is correct.Let  $s$  be the number of intratile splices. Each such splice identifies two isolated receiver tiles as one physical tile, so the union receiver has
$$r_{\mathrm{union}}=\sum_i r_i-s$$
tiles.For an intratile splice, the two port sites are original selected supports of the opposite modules and are counted in the corresponding isolated receivers by receiver locality. They become endpoints after splicing, so the union selected count loses exactly two sites:
$$t_{\mathrm{union}}=\sum_i t_i-2s.$$
For an intertile splice, the selected support used by the other module was not counted in the first module’s receiver: if it had been, receiver locality would have forced the first module’s endpoint into that same tile, contradicting that the splice is intertile.The matching edges remain the disjoint union of the  $M_i$ . Consequently,
$$\begin{aligned}
\rho_{\mathrm{union}}
&=
\left(\sum_i t_i-2s\right)
+\sum_i |M_i|
-2\left(\sum_i r_i-s\right)\\
&=
\sum_i\left(t_i+|M_i|-2r_i\right)
=
\sum_i \rho_i.
\end{aligned}$$
This is an additive statement about the corrected closed-receiver charge. It does not incorrectly add raw charges of overlapping tiles.Positive modules cannot be adjacentThe local obstruction to joining two  $+1$  modules is valid.In the  $+1$  phase, a port tile contains the port and both of its selected supports. If two such ports are spliced, the two remaining tile corners stay selected. Those two corners are adjacent to each other, and each is adjacent to one of the two splice endpoints. This violates the feasible selected-set condition because each selected corner then has more than one occupied neighbor.Hence two positive modules cannot be adjacent in the module graph.If  $c_i$  are the charges along a path, then  $c_i\le1$  and
$$c_i+c_{i+1}\le0.$$
Indeed, two  $+1$  modules are forbidden, while any nonpositive module has charge at most  $-1$ . Pairing consecutive terms gives total path charge at most zero for even paths and at most one for odd paths.For a cycle,
$$2\sum_i c_i
=
\sum_i(c_i+c_{i+1})
\le0,$$
so the total charge is nonpositive. The two-module parallel-edge cycle is included: its two adjacent-pair inequalities are the same inequality counted twice.The stronger positive-path statement is also correct. If  $p$  and  $n$  count positive and negative modules, then nonadjacency gives  $p\le n+1$ , while
$$\sum_i c_i\le p-n.$$
A positive total forces  $p=n+1$ , every negative charge to equal exactly  $-1$ , and the modules to alternate with positive modules at both ends.Surviving donors and compensationEvery  $+1$  module retains the stated degree-three donor. In the reference orientation, the donor data are
$$x=(3,2),\quad
p=(3,1),\quad
z=(2,3),\quad
q=(1,3).$$
The selected  $x$  is not a port support, including in the minimum leg-height case  $a,b\ge4$ . Therefore no splice consumes it. The guard  $q$  is not a port, and the splice hypotheses forbid unrelated foreign endpoint contacts, so its three occupied endpoint neighbors remain exactly the same. The anchor and guard remain in the same endpoint component after modules are joined.Thus each positive module has an actual capacity-one endpoint-free donor tile. Choosing one donor per positive connected network is legitimate. Two networks cannot choose the same donor tile: the tile has one selected site and one unique occupied endpoint anchor, which identifies its endpoint component.If  $N_+$  is the number of positive-charge networks, then
$$\sum_H \rho_H\le N_+.$$
Since there are  $N_+$  distinct unit donors,
$$N_+\le D,$$
and therefore the class satisfies
$$\sum_H\rho_H\le D.$$
Using the corrected identity  $\sigma=D-\rho$ , this gives
$$|T|+|M|\le \frac{mn}{2}.$$
The claimed improvement over the  $5/6$  coefficient is exactly
$$|M|-\frac56|M|=\frac16|M|.$$
This remains a class theorem; it does not claim reduction of arbitrary configurations to the modular class.Reservation-aware  $q\le5$  consequenceThe reservation argument is correct, but its logic should be stated in the strongest form.After  $B$  distinct valid reservations, at most  $B$  of the  $N_+$  selected donor units can disappear. Hence at least
$$N_+-B\ge \rho-B=q$$
distinct donor tiles remain whenever  $q=\rho-B$ .For  $q\le4$ , the earlier first-failure threshold already rules out a target-preserving failure of the mixed certificate.For  $q=5$ , if  $A<q$ , then  $F\le A<5$ , so the earlier first- $q=5$  classification applies. It forces exactly one positive-capacity resource component and one of the three remaining quota motifs:
$$\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}.$$
These motifs occupy only three or four positive-capacity physical tiles, despite having five or six slots through multiplicity. But  $q=5$  leaves at least five distinct donor tiles with positive residual capacity. Those additional positive tiles would constitute additional positive-capacity resource components or enlarge the sole component, contradicting the first- $q=5$  classification.Therefore a target-preserving local-quota failure cannot occur for  $q\le5$  in this modular class, even after arbitrary distinct valid reservations.All-length zigzag constructionThe all-length construction is consistent.For  $N$  copies of the  $w=6,a=b=4$  module:each module has  $18$  endpoints;each module has  $9$  matching edges;the total matching has  $9N$  edges;the selected-support count after the  $N-1$  splices is  $8N+2$ .The last count is consistent with each isolated copy having ten selected supports and each splice consuming two:
$$10N-2(N-1)=8N+2.$$
The alternating translation/reflection produces module charges  $+1,-1,+1,-1,\ldots$ . By the splice ledger, the connected path has charge  $1$  for odd  $N$  and  $0$  for even  $N$ .The matching uniqueness argument is valid provided the base module’s matching uniqueness is inherited. Each module’s endpoint set has even cardinality. Every intermodule splice is a bridge, and removing it leaves two sides with even numbers of endpoint vertices. A perfect matching cannot use that bridge, because each side would then have an odd number of unmatched vertices. Therefore the global perfect matching is the union of the unique module matchings, and is itself unique.The mixed-bundle exclusion is not a consequence of uniqueness alone; it uses the stated degree-three matching criterion. Under that previously established criterion, the splice preserves the required degree-three structure, and the criterion excludes mixed promotion bundles just as it excludes one-color bundles.The zigzag spacing also has the intended geometry: consecutive modules meet only at the shared port column, their retained perpendicular supports lie on opposite sides of the splice, and nonconsecutive copies are separated. Thus the all-length construction provides arbitrarily many chambers without introducing unlisted endpoint contacts.The only missing-hypothesis issue is therefore scope, not a counterexample:The extension should explicitly import the earlier uniform two-leg lemma excluding the first three donor rules, and the mixed-bundle version of the degree-three matching criterion, for every reflected and translated copy used in the zigzag.With those stated dependencies, the theorem merits ACCEPT.
